title: The Writings
hookLine: the third part of the Tanakh: poems, wisdom books and stories
carry: they praise, they doubt, they complain

lines: A KING SINGS, A FATHER WARNS.
A MAN ARGUES, A WOMAN SEARCHES.
A WIDOW GLEANS, A QUEEN KEEPS A SECRET.
cards: Turn the page past Malachi in a Jewish Bible, and the voices change. A king sings to God on a harp. A father teaches his son, and tells the lazy to go and watch the ant.
A man covered in sores argues with heaven and won't be comforted. A woman in love searches the city streets at night. A widow gleans barley behind the harvesters.
A queen keeps a secret about who she is. Exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep. And almost no one stands up to say thus saith the LORD.

teach.h: KETUVIM: EVERYTHING ELSE THAT WAS KEPT.
teach.b: Ketuvim. Writings. The Torah is the teaching, the Prophets are the voice of God through messengers, and the Writings are everything else that was kept.
Psalms, the songs and cries that run through the Jewish prayer book. Proverbs, short wisdom about tongues, money and friends. Job, a long argument about suffering that never quite settles.
Then short scrolls Jews call megillot, each tied by custom to a season: Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth on Shavuot, Lamentations on Tisha B'Av, Ecclesiastes during Sukkot, Esther on Purim.
Then Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles. What changes when you cross over? In the Prophets, God mostly speaks to people.
In the Writings, people mostly speak: to God, to each other, to themselves. They praise, they doubt, they complain, they fall in love, they grieve a city. Ecclesiastes calls it all vanity.
Esther tells its whole story without once naming God. And these books are part of the Bible too: their questions kept right next to the answers.
Printed Bibles don't all list them in the same order, and the Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, gives an order of its own.

teach.h: THE TALMUD'S ORDER STARTS WITH RUTH.
teach.b: It starts with Ruth, which is where this road goes next.
Before it does, look back at a week of endings: Micah's three verbs, a fig tree and no fear, Habakkuk's one line, not by might, hearts turning both ways, and a voice that goes on.

how: Jews pray the Psalms daily in the synagogue service and read the short scrolls of the Writings at their festivals, such as Esther on Purim and Ruth on Shavuot.

games.q: you're gathering the books of the Writings. one argues with God about suffering, one calls everything vanity, one never names God. what do you do?
o: leave out the ones that ask hard questions.
keep them all, side by side.
games.why: they're all kept. Job, Ecclesiastes and Esther sit in the Writings next to the Psalms.

practice: Say the names of the Writings, one for each slow breath, aloud or inside: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles.
Notice which name catches you, a song, a lament, a love poem, a story, then go back to it and stay there, just the name and the breath. If you pray, one line of a psalm you know can be enough.
